what_it_does: To understand how resilient a computer system is to hardware faults (bit flips caused by radiation, manufacturing defects, etc.), engineers run 'fault injection' tests — they deliberately flip bits and watch what happens. Graph processing workloads (programs that traverse networks of nodes and edges, such as social-network analysis or routing) run in a distinctive way: they iterate over the graph in rounds, touching only a subset of nodes each round. Existing fault injection tools ignore this structure and test randomly, which is both slow (most trials are redundant) and inaccurate. GraphFI exploits three properties specific to graph programs to prune the test space dramatically: it picks representative iteration rounds rather than testing all; it identifies groups of nodes whose error behavior is similar (using community detection on the graph topology) and tests only one from each group; and it uses a monotonicity property — if a fault at location X causes a severe error, faults at 'stronger' locations also will — to skip large regions of the test space. The combined result is up to 100x fewer fault injection experiments needed, with claimed equivalent accuracy.
